item.title: Introduction to PBR materials
item.description: See how Blender's Principled BSDF makes physically based materials (rough, metallic, coated, glass, subsurface and glowing), apply a downloaded PBR texture pack with Node Wrangler, and light a scene with a sky texture or an HDRI.
item.content:
Physically based rendering (PBR) means describing a surface by how it treats light: how rough it is, whether it's metal, whether light passes through it or glows from it. In this part you'll see how Blender's Principled BSDF shader does that, using a Suzanne head, a glass and a sphere as examples. Then you'll apply a downloaded PBR texture pack to a floor with Node Wrangler, see what each of its maps does, and light the floor like an outdoor scene with a sky texture and with an HDRI. It helps to know your way around Blender's interface. The video uses Blender 4.2 and renders with Cycles.

Material slots

0:23 The video starts with Suzanne, with a Subdivision Surface modifier and Shade Smooth, so the materials are easy to see.

  • Make a material. 0:39 In the Material tab of the Properties editor, click New. It looks the same as the default material until you change it. Double-click its name to rename it (the video calls it "monkey") so you can find it later 0:51; the sphere icon beside the name lists every material in the file 0:58.
  • An object can have more than one. 1:14 The + button adds material slots, and the arrows change their order. The first material covers every face until you assign another: press Tab for Edit Mode, select some faces, select a slot and click Assign 2:09.
  • Usually, stick with one. 2:30 Assigning materials to faces isn't an easy way to colour or texture regions of a model. Use one material per object unless the parts really are different materials.

The Principled BSDF

2:59 Open the Shading workspace and the new material shows as a Principled BSDF node plugged into the Material Output. It's the shader for physically based rendering: it controls how light reflects off your geometry, and simulates light bouncing inside it and, for some materials, refracting through it 4:36.

  • Render engine. 3:11 EEVEE is more like a game engine's approximation of physically based materials, though it does a good job, with ray tracing on newer computers. Cycles gives the best result 3:25. The video switches Cycles' Device to GPU Compute so it renders faster 3:33.
  • Roughness. 3:55 Turn it far down and the surface looks like shiny plastic, with small, sharp highlights. At 1 the highlights spread across the surface, like rough rubber 4:16. The default, 0.5, is in between, like dull plastic 4:29.
  • Metallic. 5:05 Set it to 1 for metal. Real things are metal or not (non-metals are called dielectrics), so it's 0 or 1, never half. A texture can make some parts metal and others not, like a metal object with dirt on it 5:11.
  • Coat. 5:44 For glossy car paint, open Coat and raise its Weight, then lower the coat's roughness 5:56. It adds a thin, glossy layer over the surface 6:16, with its own index of refraction (IOR) 6:28.

Glass and refraction

  • Turn on transmission. 6:48 Transmission lets light through and refracts it, like glass. Set Metallic to 0, bring Roughness right down and raise Transmission → Weight to 1 6:58.
  • Give it something to refract. 7:05 Glass on its own doesn't look right. Put another object behind it (the video moves a cube behind Suzanne) and you see it bent through the glass; hide it and the glass is much less convincing 7:24.
  • Index of refraction. 7:46 Different materials refract by different amounts; look the value up in a table of indices of refraction. The video guesses about 1.35 for water (tables give about 1.33).
  • A shell, not a solid. 8:08 A Solidify modifier gives the object a thin wall, so it refracts like a cup rather than a solid block of glass.
  • Make a glass. 8:37 The video models a drinking glass from a cylinder, extruded into a cup with an edge loop added, then Shade Smooth and a Subdivision Surface modifier with more levels 9:16, and an inset on the bottom to reduce artifacts 9:37. Then it gets the same material 9:44. That's all a glass needs: transmission on and roughness down 11:12. The small ripples are smoothing mistakes, but they make the glass look more real 10:55.
  • Enough light bounces. 10:14 Light passes through several walls of a glass. If Light Paths doesn't allow enough bounces, parts of it render black.

Subsurface scattering

11:37 Subsurface is what skin does with light: it goes in, bounces around inside, and comes out somewhere else. Anything organic, like skin or a leaf, does it 12:46.

  • 11:44 Set Subsurface → Weight to 1 and Roughness to 1, and put a light behind the object 12:04. Raise the subsurface Scale to let light travel further inside 12:14. (A Solidify modifier left on from the glass got in the way, so the video turns it off 12:33.)
  • 13:07 The three Radius values are the red, green and blue channels: how far each colour of light travels. Turn red to 0 and blue up, and the light coming through is blue instead of red 13:23. The surface's own colour and the Scale play a part too.
  • 13:57 Most light comes through the thinnest parts, here the ears.

Emission

  • Make an object glow. 14:03 The video adds a sphere with a new Principled BSDF, opens Emission and raises its Strength (10 is a good start) 14:27, then hides the scene's light so all the light comes from the sphere 14:33.
  • Colour the light. 14:45 The higher the strength, the whiter the object itself looks, but the light it gives off keeps the colour, just as you can colour a point, sun, spot or area light 15:08. It's how to put a practical light, one that's part of the scene, in the shape of a mesh 15:31.
  • The Emission shader 15:40 does the same with fewer settings. The Principled BSDF is the multi-tool that can do it all 16:01.

Texture maps

16:13 Sliders give a surface one value all over. For realistic texture, the video uses a PBR texture pack: a set of images that each control one property of the material across the surface.

  1. Download a texture pack. 16:35 Add a plane, then find a material on a site such as ambientCG.com (the video picks Wood Floor 044 17:01). JPEG or PNG are both fine. 2K is enough for most uses; 4K and 8K are for objects seen very close, and the files get much bigger 17:28.

  2. See what's in it. 17:47 Unzip the pack into your project's folder. It has a color map, ambient occlusion, displacement, metalness (for a few nails in the floorboards), two normal maps and roughness 18:05.

    The Sculpture garden exercise asks you to save texture packs in a folder called textures in your project folder, at 2K or smaller.

  3. Turn on Node Wrangler. 18:40 Make a new material, choose Edit → Preferences → Add-ons and enable Node Wrangler (it comes with Blender).

  4. Add a Principled setup. 18:56 Select the Principled BSDF node, press Shift+W for the Node Wrangler menu and choose Add Principled Setup. In the pack's folder, select the roughness, NormalGL, metalness, displacement, color and ambient occlusion images 19:12 (not the NormalDX map or the other files).

    19:26 Node Wrangler adds an image node for each, plugs each into the right socket of the Principled BSDF, and adds a Displacement node for the displacement image, plugged into the Material Output's Displacement. A Texture Coordinate and a Mapping node drive them all, so you can move, rotate and scale the texture in one place 19:44.

    Blender crashed during the video and the autosave didn't work, so this step was done again 19:57.

  5. Turn on displacement. 20:24 Out of the box, the Displacement node does nothing. With Cycles as the render engine, open the material's Settings → Surface: Displacement is Bump Only 20:40. Change it to Displacement and Bump. The default scale is too strong; the video starts at 0.1 20:57.

  6. Give it vertices to move. 21:06 Displacement really moves vertices, and a plane has only four. One way: set the render Feature Set to Experimental, add a Subdivision Surface modifier set to Simple and tick Adaptive Subdivision 21:21. It adds more subdivisions close to the camera and fewer far away 22:26, and shows only in the render (the scene needs a light 21:53). The other way, with the Supported feature set: add subdivisions until the displacement shows 22:45. It takes a huge number (the video's plane ends up with over 260,000 vertices) 23:17.

  7. Smooth it and tone it down. 23:28 Right-click and choose Shade Smooth, then lower the Displacement node's Scale: 0.1 is still too much, and 0.02 looks right for these planks 23:37.

  8. Mix in ambient occlusion. 24:16 The Principled BSDF has no ambient occlusion socket. Set the ambient occlusion image to sRGB, add a Mix Color node between the color map and Base Color, plug the ambient occlusion into it, set it to Multiply and raise its Factor 24:34. It adds a faint shadow in the cracks, for a little more contrast 24:44.

What each map does

  • Base color 25:09 is the flat, unlit colour of the surface.
  • Metallic 25:15 says which parts are metal and which are dielectric.
  • Roughness 25:48 says where the surface is rough and where it's shiny.
  • Normal 26:35 tells light which way to bounce at each pixel, so a flat surface catches highlights and casts small shadows as if it had detail. The video plugs the normal map straight into the surface to show what it looks like, then unplugs the displacement and moves a light close: the plane is perfectly flat but still looks grooved 27:09.
  • Displacement actually moves the surface, for extra detail 27:41.

25:32 Image nodes start as sRGB, right for the colour map. Set metallic, roughness, displacement and normal maps to Non-Color (Node Wrangler does this for you): they describe the surface, not its colour, and Blender's colour management, which can change the contrast of colours across the whole render, mustn't change them 26:03.

27:47 Game engines use the same maps, which is how they look realistic at 60 frames a second or more.

Lighting with the world

  1. Open the world's nodes. 28:49 In the Shader Editor, change Object to World. Its Background node is the same as the World properties tab: ambient light that comes from everywhere 29:03. Black is like outer space, white floods the scene with light 29:16. The video puts it back to the default grey.

  2. Add a Sky Texture. 29:39 Add a Sky Texture node (it's built into Blender) and plug its Color into the Background: a sun and sky. Sun Rotation turns the direction of the shadows; Sun Elevation sets their length 29:52. A low sun casts long shadows and turns the light from blue at midday to warm in the evening 30:14.

  3. Soften the sun. 30:28 Turn off Sun Disc for even light and much softer shadows. Or keep it and raise Sun Size to blur the shadows: less realistic, but it may look nicer 30:36. Of the sky types, the video prefers the default, Nishita 31:27.

  4. Use an HDRI instead. 31:35 Unplug the sky and add an Environment Texture node. It's like an image texture, but wraps the image around the world with equirectangular mapping, the usual format for these images 31:50. ambientCG has HDRIs too 31:57; the video downloads a 2K one of a field.

Why an HDRI lights a scene well

32:46 Opened in Photoshop, the HDRI looks duller than its preview: it's a 32-bit image, and monitors show 8 bits 32:54. Lower its exposure and the white sky doesn't just get darker: detail appears, right down to the sun's disc and the clouds around it 33:23. Raise it and there's detail in the shadows too 34:20. All that range is what makes its light on your scene so much better than a plain colour 34:45.

37:09 An HDRI is usually an EXR file (there's an HDR format too), made outdoors with special camera equipment. Film crews make them on set so visual effects artists can light 3D scenes with the same light 37:24.

  1. Light the scene with it. 34:53 Open an HDRI in the Environment Texture node (the video uses another one it had already downloaded). It wraps around the scene like a sphere and lights the objects 35:10.

  2. Hide or block the background. 35:28 To render without it, tick Film → Transparent in the render properties. Or build walls, add a camera and look through it, and check that you see neither transparent pixels nor the background, unless you plan to composite something behind 35:41.

  3. Adjust the strength. 36:14 If it isn't bright enough, raise the Background's Strength a little, to 1.25 or 2 36:20.

Wrap-up

The Principled BSDF covers most materials with a few settings: roughness and metallic for most surfaces, coat for gloss, transmission for glass, subsurface for skin and leaves, emission for things that glow. A PBR texture pack varies those settings across the surface, and Node Wrangler wires it up in one step; remember to turn on displacement and to give it vertices. Light outdoor scenes with a Sky Texture or an HDRI. The next part puts all of this together in a sculpture garden.

Check your understanding

  1. Why should Metallic usually be 0 or 1, and when would a texture make it vary?
  2. Which two settings turn the Principled BSDF into glass, and why does glass need other objects around it?
  3. Which maps in a texture pack should be Non-Color, and why?
  4. What's the difference between a normal map and displacement? What does displacement need before it works?
  5. What can an HDRI do for lighting that a plain background colour can't?
